source.book: The Art and Science of Technical Analysis
source.author: Adam Grimes

conventions: stop and limit entries mechanized as bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; price-level conditions rejected (shift test)

candidates.name: PartialProfitFractionAtFirstTarget
candidates.quote: As a matter of discipline, I take profits on between 25 and 50 percent of the position at this first profit target.
candidates.description: When open profit reaches the initial risk (the 1R first target -- entry to stop distance, in the direction of the trade), exit a fixed fraction of the position rather than the whole position or none of it. Grimes gives a range (20 to 50 percent depending on aggressiveness) rather than a single number.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at the 1R price (a scale-out), not a stop

complexity.reason: a difference test against a fixed 1R level computed once at entry, plus a partial-size exit

notes: Grimes states a range of 25-50% as his normal discipline, with 20% in rare aggressive cases and 50% when concerned about a trade; defaulted partialFraction to 0.375 (midpoint of the stated normal range) since no single number is given.
This assumes the engine's pane system supports partial exits; if not, the authoring pass should note the limitation.

candidates.name: FirstTargetCappedAtNearestSwingLevel
candidates.quote: I set my first target at one times my risk in almost all cases, the only exceptions being when that target would be beyond a very visible chart point.
candidates.description: The standard first target is 1R, but if the 1R price would lie beyond the nearest visible chart level (a recent swing high/low), use that swing level as the target instead of the full 1R distance.
candidates.pseudocode:
// long
naturalTarget = ctx.EntryPrice() + 1.0 * initialRiskDistance
nearestSwingLevel = highest(high, swingLookback)  // most recent swing high above entry, computed at entry time
targetPrice = min(naturalTarget, nearestSwingLevel)
high[0] >= targetPrice

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection to find the nearest visible chart level ahead of the 1R price, not just a fixed-window highest/lowest

notes: approximated 'a very visible chart point' as the nearest swing pivot; Grimes does not define this precisely.

candidates.name: TightenStopAfterConsecutiveFavorableCloses
candidates.quote: At this point, the second downward closing bar, the trade is working. This is a small, but very important point: once a trade is working, once the market is moving in the intended direction, tighten stops to reduce open risk.
candidates.description: Once the position has N consecutive bar closes in the trade's favor since entry, tighten the stop (reduce its distance from the market, e.g. move it toward breakeven) rather than leaving the original stop in place.
candidates.pseudocode:
// short example generalized to long: consecutive up-closes since entry
consecutiveFavorable = 0
for i = 0 to bars_since_entry: if close[i] > close[i+1] then consecutiveFavorable++ else break
consecutiveFavorable >= tightenAfterCloses  // triggers tightening the stop toward entry/breakeven
candidates.book_order_type: stop order moved closer to the market

complexity.reason: a counter of consecutive favorable closes since entry, persisted across bars

notes: Grimes's example uses exactly 2 consecutive favorable closes as the trigger point in this trade narrative; treated as the default rather than a universal rule.

candidates.name: FailureTestTimeStopIfTargetNotHit
candidates.quote: You should not have to wait more than three or four bars for the profit target to be hit, and many times it will be reached on the first bar following the entry.
candidates.description: Specific to failure-test entries (stop and target both close to entry): if the 1R first target has not been reached within N bars of entry, treat this as a warning sign and reduce or exit the position rather than waiting for the stop.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.BarsSinceEntry() >= maxBarsToTarget && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() < initialRiskDollars  // triggers reducing/exiting the position
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (discretionary reduce/exit, mechanized as a time-based exit)

complexity.reason: a bar-count-since-entry test combined with an open-profit comparison

notes: Scoped by Grimes specifically to failure-test trades, where stop and target both sit close to entry; the authoring pass should decide whether to gate this on a FailureTest identity or leave it general with a note.

candidates.name: FailureTestStopAtSwingExtreme
candidates.quote: The stop in this trade should be located at or around (within a few pennies of) the previous trend high... Placing the stop inside the previous extreme will result in a rare stop-out where the trade is still valid, but the reduced slippage on nearly all exits will more than compensate.
candidates.description: For a failure-test entry, place the initial stop AT (or just inside) the swing extreme the pattern is testing, rather than beyond it with a safety buffer. This deliberately accepts a few extra premature stop-outs in exchange for less slippage on the much larger set of trades where the stop is actually hit.
candidates.book_order_type: stop order placed inside (not beyond) the tested swing extreme

complexity.reason: depends on the swing extreme the failure test is built on being already located by the pattern's own pivot detection

candidates.likely_existing_rule: StopBeyondSignalBar / InitialStopBeyondSwingAtEntry (this is the opposite convention: inside, not beyond)
notes: This is a deliberate contrast with the usual 'stop beyond the swing extreme' rule: Grimes argues for stopping inside the extreme on failure tests specifically, to cut slippage. Flag this to the authoring pass since it conflicts with the more common convention.

candidates.name: ExitPullbackIfFlatAfterNBars
candidates.quote: If this assumption is incorrect, the market may simply go flat after the trade is entered, without a significant move up or down. This is strong evidence that the market has temporarily found equilibrium and that whatever edge there might have been in the trade is now gone.
candidates.description: If a pullback trade has produced no meaningful directional movement (bar ranges stay compressed, no progress toward target or stop) within N bars of entry, scratch the trade for a small win or loss rather than continuing to hold.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (discretionary scratch, mechanized as a time+range exit)

complexity.reason: needs a bars-since-entry counter and an ATR-scaled measure of how far price has moved since entry

notes: Grimes gives no exact bar count for 'too long to sit in a simple pullback'; defaulted maxFlatBars to 6 as a sensible guess for a swing-trade pullback and said so here.

candidates.name: LongConsolidationNearExtremeFilter
candidates.quote: Many times a market will show a series of consistent consolidations (say five to eight bars), and then will consolidate near the trend extreme in a much longer consolidation, perhaps three or four times the normal length... it often sets up a good countertrend trade on a failure test.
candidates.description: Context filter for countertrend failure-test entries: favor the setup when the consolidation near the trend extreme is markedly longer (a multiple of the typical recent consolidation length) than the consolidations that preceded it earlier in the trend.
candidates.pseudocode:
// ratio of the current consolidation's bar count to the typical recent consolidation length; both are bar counts, so this passes the shift test
currentConsolidationLength >= extremeLengthMultiple * typicalConsolidationLength

complexity.reason: needs a consolidation/range detector to measure consolidation length at all, plus tracking the typical length of prior consolidations in the trend

notes: 'consolidation length' itself needs a working definition (e.g. runs of overlapping bars or bars inside a tight range); this candidate assumes that primitive exists elsewhere in the corpus.

candidates.name: StopBeyondHigherTimeframeRangeForLowerTimeframeEntry
candidates.quote: If using some of these patterns, it may make sense to adjust the stop to respect the limits of the higher time frame pattern. In other words, if positioning in a daily range using a 30-minute Anti, perhaps set the stop outside the daily range. This will result in a much smaller position size, but it will be a position size that respects the reality of the higher time frame market structure.
candidates.description: When a lower-timeframe pattern is traded inside a higher-timeframe range, the initial stop should sit beyond the higher-timeframe range boundary rather than just beyond the lower-timeframe setup, so the trade isn't stopped out by noise that is still inside the larger structure.
candidates.pseudocode:
// long; higher-timeframe range approximated by a longer lookback on the same bars per the multi-timeframe convention
higherTimeframeRangeLow = lowest(low, higherTimeframeLookback)
initialStopPrice = min(patternStopPrice, higherTimeframeRangeLow - stopBuffer * ctx.MinMove())
low[0] <= initialStopPrice
candidates.book_order_type: stop order beyond the higher-timeframe range

complexity.reason: requires approximating a higher (e.g. daily) range from a longer lookback on the entry (e.g. 30-minute) bars, per the multi-timeframe convention

notes: higherTimeframeLookback of 78 approximates one daily session on 30-minute bars (13 bars/session x ~6 sessions for a multi-day daily range); this is a rough multi-timeframe stand-in per the mining brief's convention, not something Grimes specifies numerically.

candidates.name: OverExitOnFailedAddOn
candidates.quote: This example also raised the possibility of adding to an existing position. This is a good plan in many cases, but it also makes sense to aggressively adjust the position if that second entry fails by exiting more than was added. In other words, if you were holding 5,000 shares from C and added 2,000 at D, you would exit more than 2,000 on the failure of D.
candidates.description: When a pyramided add-on to an existing position fails (the add-on's own stop/failure condition triggers), exit more size than was added at that add-on -- reducing the original core position too, not just closing out the add-on.
candidates.pseudocode:
// requires position-history state: size added at the most recent add-on
addOnFailureTriggered && exitSize > mostRecentAddOnSize  // exitSize computed as overExitMultiple * mostRecentAddOnSize
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (position-management rule on a stop/failure trigger)

complexity.reason: needs cross-bar position-history state: the size of the most recent add-on and a way to detect that add-on's failure

notes: Grimes gives no exact over-exit ratio, only that it should exceed the added amount; defaulted overExitMultiple to 1.5x the add-on size and said so here.

candidates.name: ExitOnExtremeFavorableRangeExpansion
candidates.quote: This is the May 2010 Flash Crash. If you are ever holding a position into such an exceptional move, cover part or all of the position into the move. Do not be greedy and do not play for a one-in-a-million event. On those very rare occasions when the market offers windfall profits, take them.
candidates.description: If the current bar's move in the position's favor is an extreme outlier relative to normal volatility (range far beyond a multiple of ATR), take the windfall by covering part or all of the position on that bar rather than assuming continuation.
candidates.pseudocode:
// long
marketPosition() == 1 && (high[0] - low[0]) >= extremeRangeMultiple * atr(atrLength) && close[0] > ctx.EntryPrice()  // triggers covering part/all of the position
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (discretionary windfall exit, mechanized as a range-vs-ATR outlier test)

complexity.reason: a single bar's range compared against a multiple of its ATR, plus a position-direction check

notes: Grimes's example (the May 2010 Flash Crash) is an extreme outlier; extremeRangeMultiple of 4x ATR is a guessed threshold for 'exceptional move,' not a number he gives.

candidates.name: SpringMinimumPenetrationDepth
candidates.quote: Note that this is a classic Wyckoff spring, though the best examples of springs should penetrate previous support more decisively... E is a small spring, and may not be a realistic entry as it penetrates previous support by only a few cents.
candidates.description: A spring (dip below prior support followed by recovery) is a more reliable entry when the penetration below support is a meaningful distance (scaled to volatility) rather than a token few ticks. This is a quality filter on the Spring primitive defined elsewhere in the corpus, not a redefinition of Spring itself.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (quality filter on an existing entry pattern)

complexity.reason: a difference (penetration distance) compared against a fraction of ATR, once the Spring's support level and low are known

notes: Assumes 'Spring' (dip below support, then recovery) is already defined as a primitive elsewhere in the Grimes corpus (Chapter 6's trading templates, per this chapter's summary); minPenetrationAtrFraction of 0.25 ATR is a guessed threshold since Grimes only says 'a few cents' is too little.

rejected.quote: Understanding bigger picture money flows between markets. In stocks this might mean understanding the difference in performance between domestic and foreign indexes...
rejected.reason: data the engine cannot have (other symbols, sectors, cross-market comparisons)

rejected.quote: There is more potential for extreme volatility and large surprise moves near the end of trends, so it may make sense to trade some of these on smaller size and portfolio risk.

it probably makes sense to do these failure test trades on smaller risk... Trading these failure tests on smaller size, perhaps half the size of normal, with-trend trades, is a prudent risk management step.
it is important to have profit-taking orders working all the time, good until canceled and outside of regular trading hours.
rejected.reason: order-placement/execution logistics, not a bar-level price condition

rejected.quote: You have to decide how reactive you wish to be to small signals like this.
reproducing (edited) comments from my daily market report that show the evolution of my thought process and the risk management plan at different points in the move.
rejected.reason: discretionary narrative trade management (Silver parabolic climax); the specific mechanized actions (tighten stop, ratchet stop) restate the generic trailing/breakeven stop primitives already defined elsewhere, no new numeric rule

chapter_summary: Chapter 10 works through roughly 20 real trade examples (pullbacks, failure tests, parabolic climaxes, the Anti, breakouts at support/resistance) that mostly reapply the trading templates and primitives from Chapter 6 (pullback, complex pullback, failure test, spring, upthrust, Anti, climax, Keltner band reads) and were summarized here rather than re-mined bar by bar, per the mining brief. New material extracted: the 25-50% partial-exit fraction at the 1R first target and its aggressive/conservative variants; capping the 1R target at the nearest visible swing level; tightening the stop after consecutive favorable closes; a specific 3-4 bar time stop for failure tests that haven't reached target; the counterintuitive rule of placing a failure-test stop INSIDE (not beyond) the tested swing extreme to cut slippage; scratching a pullback that goes flat after entry; a consolidation-length ratio filter for countertrend failure tests near a trend extreme; setting the stop beyond a higher-timeframe range when trading a lower-timeframe pattern inside it; over-exiting (more than the added size) when a pyramided add-on fails; taking a windfall exit on an extreme single-bar favorable range expansion; and a minimum-penetration-depth quality filter on the Spring pattern. All position-sizing-by-pattern-risk statements (half-size failure tests, smaller size near trend termination) were rejected as position sizing, consistent with Chapter 9's treatment.
